newsitem.title: USA: Dollar gains after Rubin, Clinton support ahead of G7.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gains after Rubin, Clinton support ahead of G7.

text.p: The dollar rose Friday against the German mark and recouped losses vs. the Japanese yen as Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reaffirmed support for a strong dollar.

Briefing reporters on the upcoming meeting of finance ministers from the Group of Seven (G7) wealthy industrial nations this weekend, Rubin said that U.S. policy for a strong dollar remains unchanged.

Shortly following Rubin's remarks was a meeting between President Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto. The leaders showed no apparent friction over Japan's growing trade surplus with the United States, and that pushed the dollar to a session high against the yen and mark, traders said.
Clinton later told a news conference he does not want a weak dollar simply to improve the United States' trade position or foreign exchange rates thrown "out of whack".

Currency dealers had been concerned Japan's bilateral trade surplus, which rose in March for the sixth consecutive month, could encourage government officials to support a stronger yen at the expense of the dollar.
Rubin also repeated past remarks that he shared Japan's concerns about the weakness of the yen and that currencies should not be used as trade tools.
"The Rubin comments were exactly as expected. I don't think he said anything different than he has said all along," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank.
The dollar rose to 1.7275 marks by the U.S. close from 1.7150 at Thursday's close and 126.30 yen from 126.08.

The dollar's rise above 1.72 marks was sparked by a report from Bridge News that quoted Deutsche Bank chief economist Norbert Walter as saying the United States, Germany and Japan would tolerate a dollar rise to 1.80 marks and 130 yen.
However, the dollar's move higher quickly lost momentum when traders realised the report's source was not a German government economist, as initially thought.

"I think it got the ball rolling, but it really shouldn't have," said James Powers, a vice president at West Deutsche Landesbank Girozentale. "There were just a lot of (orders to buy dollars) that were above 1.72 marks."

In early U.S. trade, the dollar and mark were jostled by conflicting comments from German central bankers and politicians regarding the likelihood of the Europe Union meetings its 1999 deadline for a single currency.

Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said the prospect of a delay should not be "categorically ruled out" while German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said Bonn would never accept a delay in the timetable.

In Japan, the dollar weakened against the yen as Japanese government bond futures fell more than a full point on worries Japanese life insurer Nissan Mutual Life Insurance might be forced to sell its assets, including yen bonds, after the Finance Ministry ordered it to halt operations.
In other trading, the dollar rose to 1.4695 Swiss francs from 1.4608 and Canadian $1.3976 from C$1.3926. The British pound inched lower to $1.6245 from $1.6265.
